record.source: Resolution of the Auraria convention, 15 April 1859, printed in the Cherry Creek Pioneer, 23 April 1859: from the 43rd parallel at the 102nd meridian west to the 110th, south to the 37th parallel, east to the 102nd; the organic act ratified on 24 October 1859 kept those bounds (J. C. Smiley, Semi-centennial History of the State of Colorado, 1913); Colorado Territory from 28 February 1861 (the Newberry)
record.note: The convention's text reckons the meridians "from Washington city"; every later text, and this map, reads them from Greenwich. The organic act's own text was not found: its bounds rest on Smiley. Not yet reviewed by the owner.

ended.text: The United States created Oklahoma Territory from Indian Territory and unorganized federal territory (the Oklahoma panhandle or Public Land Strip).
ended.cite: ("Proclamation," Weekly Oklahoma State Capital [newspaper], 7 June 1890; U.S. Stat., vol. 26, ch. 182[1890], sec. 4/p. 83; Morris, 116-118; Van Zandt, 139-140)

warnings: the sources disagree on Washington Territory: the Newberry dates it from 14 February 1859 ("Washington Territory gained non-county area when the state of Oregon was created from Oregon Territory. Non-County Area 2 included parts of present Idaho, Montana, and Wyoming."), and OpenHistoricalMap has San Juan Boundary Dispute (relation 2888729) held by British Empire on this date, until 1 November 1866; the map draws the Newberry's polygon
alt_text: Parchment map, 1 January 1860, states and territories, framed on a box of the continent, titled "Jefferson Territory, 1860". Shaded: Kansas Territory, Nebraska Territory and 2 more in green. Hatched in rust: proposed territory (not recognized). Named on the map: Nebraska Territory, New Mexico Territory, Utah Territory, Jefferson Territory and Kansas Territory.
